tagline.text: A 1921 neoclassical bridge over the Pasig River linking Binondo and Intramuros

location.label: Location
location.text: Manila, between Quintin Paredes Road in Binondo and Padre Burgos Avenue in Ermita

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (crossing the bridge is free; snacks and transport included, half-day basis)

children.text: Jones Bridge, completed in 1921, is one of the best-known bridges over Manila's Pasig River, linking Chinatown's Binondo with the walled city of Intramuros. Destroyed in the war and restored in 2019, it has regained its stone-style balustrades, lamp posts and statues, and is now a popular spot for evening strolls and night views.

Jones Bridge spans the Pasig River in Manila and connects the Binondo and San Nicolas districts on the north bank with Ermita and Intramuros on the south bank. Its formal name is the William A. Jones Memorial Bridge, honoring William Atkinson Jones, the U.S. congressman who wrote the 1916 Philippine Autonomy Act, known as the Jones Law. The south end sits near the Manila Central Post Office and Plaza Lawton, and the north end near Plaza Moraga and Escolta, so it is a natural crossing point when you explore old Manila on foot.

The site was originally occupied by the Spanish-era Puente de España (Bridge of Spain). Completed in 1875, it was damaged in 1914 when floods weakened its central pier; a temporary steel truss was installed and plans for a new bridge began. The new bridge was built one block downriver from the Spanish bridge: construction started in 1919, it was finished in 1920 and opened in 1921. The Filipino architect Juan M. Arellano designed it in a neoclassical and Beaux-Arts style inspired by the Pont Alexandre III in Paris, with three reinforced-concrete arches. At the time it was regarded as the grandest and most monumental bridge ever built over the Pasig.

In February 1945, during the Battle of Manila, retreating Japanese forces blew up the bridges over the Pasig, and Jones Bridge collapsed. During the Japanese occupation it had also been called the Banzai Bridge. It was rebuilt in 1946 as a simple steel-girder structure without the old ornaments and statues, and for decades it served only as a practical crossing. It was partly refurbished in 1998 for the Philippine Centennial, and in 2019 a restoration funded by about ₱20,000,000 in donations brought it closer to its original look; it reopened on November 24, 2019.

Today Jones Bridge is more than a traffic link; it is a place to enjoy on foot. The light-colored, stone-style balustrades with gold accents, the European-style lamp posts and the statues at the four corners make it great for photos, and when the lamps come on at dusk their light reflects on the Pasig. On June 7, 2025, a lighting ceremony marked the 50th anniversary of Philippine–China relations and the revival of Binondo, and a weekly weekend lights show has since been reported. Hours and schedules can change, so check the latest announcements before you go. Crossing the bridge itself takes only a few minutes on foot, so it works best not as a stand-alone destination but as the connecting piece of a day that takes in Binondo's food streets, the Escolta heritage street and Intramuros. This guide covers what to see on the bridge, a walking order, how to get there, nearby connections and what to watch out for.

blocks.title: The four La Madre Filipina statues

children.text: On the four corners at the ends of the bridge stand statues called La Madre Filipina, which portray the young nation as a mother. They are named Gratitude, Democracy, Progress and Justice. Gratitude was moved to Rizal Park after the war and returned in 2019, the destroyed Democracy was replaced with a replica in 2019, and replicas of Progress and Justice were installed in June 2021. Finding each statue and comparing them is a small pleasure of its own.

blocks.title: Neoclassical balustrades and European-style lamp posts

children.text: In the 2019 restoration the balustrades were repainted in light colors with gold accents, and Beaux-Arts-style lamp posts were added. The lamp design is credited to the architect Jerry Acuzar, and the posts are reported to be made of resin to withstand moisture and sea air. The design is often compared with the Pont Alexandre III in Paris. By day the decorative details are the attraction; by night it is the lights.

From the bridge you look upriver toward the old buildings of Escolta and the direction of Binondo, and downriver toward the walls of Intramuros. As the lamps come on at dusk, light spreads across the water, which draws many photographers and often wedding photo shoots. For safety and traffic reasons, avoid standing in the middle of the roadway and take your photos from the sidewalk.

In June 2025 a lighting ceremony sponsored by the federation of Chinese-Filipino chambers of commerce was held, and a show that lights up the bridge every weekend has been reported since. It is part of the Binondo revival project meant to draw people to the area. Times, days and whether it is running can change often, so check the latest announcements from the Manila city government or the organizers.

A newly built riverside promenade, the Pasig River Esplanade, runs near the bridge. The section from the Manila Central Post Office to Jones Bridge opened in January 2024, followed by the stretches from Jones Bridge to Plaza Mexico and from Plaza Mexico to Fort Santiago. Walking down to the riverside path lets you stroll toward the walls of Intramuros one step away from the city noise.

The Pasig River Ferry passes beneath Jones Bridge on its way to the Escolta station. Watching a ferry glide under the bridge from above is a sight in itself, and riding it, if it is running, is a nice experience. As of 2026 it is reported to be free with a valid ID under MMDA operation, but routes and operating hours can change, so confirm on site.

blocks.title: The story of the Puente de España

children.text: Jones Bridge was built to replace the old Spanish bridge one block upriver. The Spanish-era bridge, the American-period neoclassical bridge, the postwar steel bridge and the 2019 restoration all overlap in one place, so you can read Manila's modern history in a single bridge. Walking tours with local guides often add this story along the way.

items.title: A 1–2 hour bridge walk
items.subtitle: From the Central Post Office across Jones Bridge to Binondo

children.text: Start in front of the Manila Central Post Office. The south end of Jones Bridge is right next to the building, so it is hard to get lost.
Look over the statues at the south corners, then cross the bridge slowly along the sidewalk. Take in the balustrade details, the lamp posts and the boats passing on the river.
At the north end, look alternately toward Escolta and toward Binondo. If you have time, glance over a few of Escolta's old buildings.
Stroll the riverside and take photos at dusk. If you return to the bridge just as the lamps come on, you can see it at night.
Head to the restaurant streets of Binondo and finish with dinner.
In November–January the sun sets around 6 p.m., so if you want the night view, arrive a little earlier. Walking the bridge itself is short, so what you pair it with before and after matters.

items.title: A half-day old-town connection
items.subtitle: From Intramuros across Jones Bridge to Binondo

children.text: Begin the morning in Intramuros, starting with places such as Fort Santiago or San Agustin Church.
Have lunch at a restaurant inside Intramuros, or cross Jones Bridge to Binondo and eat there.
Walk across Jones Bridge and stroll Escolta Street to the north. Feel the atmosphere of the old town on a street lined with historic buildings.
Enjoy a dessert or snack in Binondo's Chinatown.
Return to Jones Bridge around dusk and watch the lamps come on.
Midday is hot and there is little shade, so bring a hat and water, and mixing in a Grab ride between stops will save your energy.
In Metro Manila you can walk toward Jones Bridge from LRT-1 Carriedo Station or Central Terminal Station. The Pasig River Ferry's Escolta station connects with Carriedo Station.

If you take a taxi or Grab, set Manila Central Post Office or Escolta as the destination and you will be dropped near the bridge. Fares vary widely with distance and traffic, so check the price in the app first.
The Manila Central Post Office is the starting point of the Pasig River Esplanade, so getting out in front of the post office and walking to the bridge is the easiest way.

items.title: After arriving by air at Manila's airport

children.text: From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Jones Bridge, a taxi or Grab is the most convenient option, but heavy traffic can make the trip long.
If you have luggage, drop it at your accommodation first and visit the bridge with light gear.
Traffic in Manila is hard to predict by day and hour, so plan generous time.
The ferry passes beneath Jones Bridge and stops at the Escolta station. It is reported to be free with a valid ID and to run during daytime hours from Monday to Saturday.
Station locations and whether the service is running can change, so confirm on site.
Intramuros, Escolta and Binondo are all within walking distance of one another.
In the heat of the day, mix in a tricycle or Grab, and always confirm the fare before you ride.

The dry season from November to May is the best time to walk the bridge. December to February is relatively cool and a midday walk is easier. March to May gets very hot, so it is better to start late in the afternoon.

The best time of day is after about 4 p.m., when the sun begins to sink. You can see both the dusk views and the lamp-lit night scene while avoiding the midday glare. If the weekend lights show is running, aim for the evening.

For lodging you can choose hotels inside Intramuros, in Ermita and Malate, or near Binondo. Staying in Binondo or around Escolta puts you within walking distance of the bridge, but city traffic is busy and the area feels different at night than by day, so read recent reviews.

Food centers on Binondo, north of Jones Bridge. Dumplings, noodles, hopia and milk tea from Chinese-Filipino cuisine are famous, and on the Intramuros side to the south there are restaurants serving traditional Filipino dishes. It is hard to eat on the bridge itself and there are few street vendors, so have your meals on the streets at either end.
The bridge is great for photos, but the sidewalk is not wide, so stand to one side and avoid blocking passersby and traffic.
If you are aiming for dusk, arrive around 4 to 5 p.m. to see both the daytime scene and the night view.
To appreciate the lamp posts and statues, walk slowly along the railing and look up and down.
The bridge is a small destination. Plan your day around Escolta, Binondo and Intramuros together to make it worthwhile.
Bring water, a hat and sunscreen in the heat of the day. There is little shade on the bridge and the riverside path.
The weekend lights show's schedule and whether it is running can change, so check the latest announcements before you go.
Book a Grab at a safe spot on a main road, and check the plate number before you get in.
Do not lean out over the river railing, and do not enter the water or swim.
This is Manila's busy old town. Pickpocketing and phone snatching are common, so hold your phone firmly when taking photos and do not wander alone into quiet riverside corners after dark.
The bridge carries four lanes of traffic, so move only along crosswalks and sidewalks and do not take photos from the roadway.
The Pasig River is not suitable for swimming, and the Coast Guard has banned swimming near the river in the past. Do not lean over the railing.
Wear your bag in front and keep valuables and large amounts of cash out of sight.
Weekend lights shows and events draw crowds and can clog nearby roads. Check the latest announcements for traffic control on event days.
Bridge operations, nearby construction and which Esplanade sections are open can change, so follow local guidance.
